extracted.intended_audience: machine learning / computer science researchers, conference organizers, program chairs, and reviewers interested in peer-review process quality
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluative criteria for measuring randomness and consistency in conference peer-review (motivated by the NIPS duplicated-committee experiment). Useful for researchers, PC chairs, and organizers assessing review reliability and designing experiments to quantify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance consistency / disagreement rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the fraction of papers on which two independent reviewing bodies disagree about acceptance (NIPS observed a 25.9% disagreement in paper fate among 166 duplicated papers, which translates into ≈57% disagreement of the accepted lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute both (a) fraction of duplicated papers with differing accept/reject outcomes and (b) fraction of one committee's accepted list that would be rejected by the other (for NIPS: 43/166 = 25.9% differing fates, but 21/37 ≈ 57% of accepted papers from one committee were rejected by the other). Report confidence intervals (e.g., NIPS reports a 95% CI of 40–75% for the stability of accepted papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance rate as determinant of expected disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The target acceptance rate (e.g., each committee tasked with 22.5% acceptance) affects the baseline expected disagreement between independent committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed disagreement to the expectation under a purely random selection given the same acceptance rate (example: at a 22.5% acceptance rate, purely random committees would disagree on 77.5% of their acceptance lists on average). Use this to contextualize whether observed disagreement is closer to random or to an ideal consistent process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability/probability an accepted paper survives a rerun
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the probability that a paper accepted in one run would also be accepted if the review process were rerun independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the duplicated-review experiment or modeled variances to compute the chance an accepted paper remains accepted on reruns; present uncertainty (e.g., NIPS's estimate with 95% CI 40–75%). This is a direct measure of the practical stability of acceptances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple binary model (half poor, half coin-flip)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rough model where half the submissions are reliably rejected and the other half are decided by an unbiased coin flip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a rule-of-thumb to explain large observed randomness, but recognize it misses gradations (e.g., some very good papers have >50% acceptance chance). Treat as an illustrative baseline rather than a full description of the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messy middle model (clear accepts/rejects + random middle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition submissions into clear accepts, clear rejects, and a middle band that is largely decided at random. The proportions of each band determine observed disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit parameterizations to observed data. Examples from the post: (a) half clear rejects and the rest random; (b) 7% of all papers are clear accepts (≈30% of accepted papers) and 93% are random; (c) 6% clear accepts, 25% clear rejects, remainder random. Use these variants to reason about how much of the corpus is reliably decided vs. noisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noisy scoring model: within-paper vs between-paper variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Model each paper with a true score v and each review as v plus noise; reviewer scores come from N(v, sigma_within^2) and true paper scores from N(0, sigma_between^2). The ratio sigma_within / sigma_between governs expected disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate sigma_within and sigma_between from review-score data (e.g., three reviews per paper averaged). The NIPS observation is consistent with sigma_within being between one and four times sigma_between. Use these estimates to predict expected disagreement without duplicating committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold-based decision zones (accept/reject/debate cutoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees effectively used score thresholds: almost everything above ~6.5 was accepted, almost everything below ~6 was rejected, and papers in between were debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or auditing decisions, treat these cutoffs as operational decision thresholds. Examine the distribution of average scores around the thresholds to understand how much debate/uncertainty remains and how sensitive outcomes are to review noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confidence-weighted scores (procedural detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Committees used a confidence-weighted score in addition to raw scores, though the blog post sets this detail aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If available, include reviewer confidence in analyses or models; otherwise, note that ignoring confidence is a simplification. When reconstructing models from released data, be explicit whether confidence weighting is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: double-blind reviewing reduces bias but may lower consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-blind reviewing likely decreases consistency (by reducing bias toward established researchers) but improves fairness; consistency is not the only goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate review-format changes (e.g., adopting double-blind) not solely on their effect on consistency but also on bias reduction and equity. Recommend balancing consistency metrics with measures of fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run controlled experiments on review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and run experiments (e.g., duplicated review assignments) to quantify randomness and other properties of peer-review and related selection processes (the NIPS experiment is an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, duplicate a subset of assignments and compare independent outcomes; ensure fairness (e.g., accept if either committee accepts) and account for logistical overhead. Use experiments to inform policy changes (e.g., for graduate admissions or conference formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical variance measurement without duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Every conference can measure within-paper and between-paper variance in reviewer scores to estimate expected randomness without needing a duplicated-committee experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate per-paper reviewer-score variance (sigma_within) and across-paper variance of true score estimates (sigma_between). Use the ratio to predict likely disagreement levels under the noisy scoring model. This provides a low-overhead diagnostic for review process noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive acceptance policy for duplicated-review experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When running duplicated-review experiments, adopt a fairness rule such as accepting any paper accepted by either committee (NIPS used this rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an inclusive final acceptance rule to avoid harming authors during the experiment. Be transparent about the policy and account for it when interpreting disagreement statistics (the duplicated-experiment design and final policy both affect observed outcomes).
